headline: Funding flows. Tactical tests. Space strategies.
deck: This week highlights significant funding rounds and military developments in the space sector.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M for co-orbital security
stories.body: True Anomaly has secured $190 million in a Series C funding round aimed at enhancing its co-orbital security capabilities. The company’s valuation now sits at $1.6 billion, underscoring the growing demand for space domain awareness technologies. With the Department of Defense increasingly focused on securing space assets, True Anomaly is well-positioned to capitalize on this trend.
stories.soWhat: If the DoD is pulling through for you, it might be time to start thinking about how to scale quickly.

stories.head: Special Ops tests mobile satellite imagery platform
stories.body: The U.S. Special Operations Forces are currently testing a mobile platform that provides direct access to satellite imagery, integrating tactical operations with real-time data. This move reflects a broader trend of military units adopting commercial technologies, including apps, to enhance situational awareness on the field. The implications for future battlefield strategies could be significant.
stories.soWhat: When the military starts using apps for tactical decisions, it’s only a matter of time before they start asking for user reviews.

stories.head: Creotech plans $118M satellite factory investment
stories.body: Creotech, the Polish aerospace company, is planning to raise $118 million to build a new satellite manufacturing facility. This investment is notable for Poland, a country that is still developing its aerospace capabilities, and could position Creotech as a key player in the European satellite market. The emphasis on local manufacturing aligns with broader European goals for strategic autonomy in space.
stories.soWhat: If Creotech can pull this off, it might just prove that you don't need to be a tech giant to make a dent in the satellite market.

talent.statLabel: Week-over-week growth in resumes from primes to Series B/C
talent.head: Talent is leaving big-aero — and it's not about money
talent.body: Compensation is not the gating factor. The complaint, almost universally, is schedule risk — the inability to ship anything quickly, the half-decade gap between joining and seeing flight hardware, the meeting that exists to schedule the meeting. The startups absorbing this talent will, in two years, be hard to compete with on a level playing field.
